learningObjectives: Differentiate synaptic, structural, intrinsic and network plasticity.
Explain LTP, LTD and homeostatic plasticity at a conceptual level.
Apply plasticity principles to psychotherapy and rehabilitation.
Recognise how plasticity can maintain both adaptive and maladaptive patterns.

anatomy.label: Long-term potentiation
anatomy.detail: Repeated coordinated activity can strengthen synaptic responses through NMDA-dependent calcium signalling, AMPA-receptor trafficking and downstream molecular change.
anatomy.clinical: LTP is one mechanism relevant to learning, but it is not a complete explanation of memory.

anatomy.label: Long-term depression
anatomy.detail: Different activity patterns can reduce synaptic strength, supporting refinement, forgetting and flexible updating.
anatomy.clinical: Weakening old predictions may be as important as strengthening new ones in therapy.

anatomy.label: Structural plasticity
anatomy.detail: Dendritic spines, axonal boutons and myelin can change with experience over hours to months.
anatomy.clinical: Structural change is constrained by age, health, stress, sleep and repeated practice.

anatomy.label: Homeostatic plasticity
anatomy.detail: Cells adjust excitability and receptor expression to prevent activity from drifting too high or too low.
anatomy.clinical: Homeostatic compensation can blunt treatment effects or stabilise networks after perturbation.

anatomy.label: Systems consolidation
anatomy.detail: Over time, memories become represented through changing interactions among hippocampal and cortical systems.
anatomy.clinical: Sleep and repeated retrieval support consolidation and integration.

interaction.title: Neuroplasticity sequence
interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to see how the system changes over time.

stages.label: Engage
stages.text: Experience activates a pattern of synapses and networks.

stages.label: Tag
stages.text: Salient or repeated activity triggers molecular plasticity signals.

stages.label: Remodel
stages.text: Receptors, synapses, excitability and structure change.

stages.label: Consolidate
stages.text: Sleep, retrieval and repetition stabilise useful network patterns.

quizBank.question: What is long-term potentiation?
options: A durable increase in synaptic efficacy after particular activity patterns
Immediate growth of an entire brain region
quizBank.explanation: LTP is a sustained strengthening of synaptic transmission.

quizBank.question: Plasticity can be maladaptive because it may:
options: Strengthen avoidance, addiction, sensitisation or chronic pain patterns
quizBank.explanation: Experience-dependent learning can stabilise harmful as well as helpful patterns.

quizBank.question: Homeostatic plasticity primarily helps neural systems:
options: Maintain activity within a workable range
quizBank.explanation: Homeostatic mechanisms counter prolonged shifts in activity.

quizBank.question: Which factor supports consolidation of new learning?
quizBank.explanation: Retrieval and sleep support stabilisation and integration.

quizBank.question: A clinically realistic view of plasticity is that change is:
options: Possible but constrained by biology, context and repetition
quizBank.explanation: Plasticity remains possible across life but is not unconstrained.
